::: {.why}
The book's realised risk moves by a factor you measured last night, which means the position size you chose in week 13 has been implicitly changing every month without you deciding anything.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Implement portfolio-level volatility targeting using the covariance estimator rather than a realised trailing number, and say why that is different.
- Report the effect on realised volatility stability, and the turnover the targeting itself generates.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Add `target_volatility()` to qlib/portfolio.py, scaling the weight vector so the predicted portfolio volatility from qlib/risk.py matches a target. Using the forecast rather than the trailing realisation is the difference between a forward-looking and a backward-looking control, and it changes the lag by roughly the estimator's halflife.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Measure both sides: report the standard deviation of rolling realised volatility with and without targeting, and the additional turnover the scaling creates. Then cap the leverage and show what the cap does in the highest-volatility periods.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write down the one failure mode: volatility targeting delevers into a drawdown, so it locks in losses in a fast reversal. Note when that has happened historically in your own sample.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The book is sized to a volatility target computed from the risk model's forecast rather than from trailing realised volatility, with an explicit leverage cap and the added turnover reported.
:::
